edge_cases.scenario: A consumer with a common name (or a Jr./Sr. father-son pair, or a near-identical SSN) finds a collection account on her report that belongs to a different real person — a classic 'mixed file.' She tells the intake that 'this account is not mine at all.' No crime, no impostor, and she cannot truthfully file an FTC IdentityTheft.gov affidavit or a police report.
edge_cases.gap_description: The dispositive THRESHOLD checklist item routes any 'the account is NOT HERS AT ALL' claim to the § 1681c-2 identity-theft block, which requires an identity theft report. Mixed-file/similar-name cases — one of the most frequent categories of FCRA disputes — are not identity theft, cannot satisfy 1681c-2(a), and would be misrouted: the consumer is told to file an identity-theft report she cannot honestly file, and the correct track (§ 1681i reinvestigation against the CRA plus § 1681e(b) reasonable-procedures claim against the CRA, with the furnisher's § 1681s-2(b) duty to check identifiers) is not surfaced. The node's threshold wording is over-inclusive as drafted; this is the converse of the previously fixed under-inclusion.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer pulls her own report, sees a charged-off balance she already paid, disputes through Equifax, the furnisher parrots its internal records and verifies, and the error stays. The tradeline was never pulled by any lender, employer, or insurer during the relevant period; she was not denied credit and has no out-of-pocket loss, but wants statutory and punitive damages for a willful violation in federal court.
edge_cases.gap_description: The remedies note affirmatively states that willful violations open statutory damages ($100–$1,000) 'without proof of actual loss.' Post-TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021), a consumer whose inaccurate information was never disseminated to a third party generally lacks Article III standing for concrete harm even on a willful/statutory-damages theory, and such suits are routinely dismissed. The node's own text, applied as encoded, tells a large and common class of consumers (self-monitoring, no publication) that they have a viable willful claim when the federal case is likely to be dismissed at the threshold. Dissemination/concrete-harm is not in the checklist at all.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputed an inaccurate tradeline through TransUnion in early 2022; the furnisher verified it and the error has sat on her report ever since. She consults now, in 2026, having only recently learned furnishers have FCRA duties. The item is still being reported inaccurately today.
edge_cases.gap_description: Checklist item 9 makes the § 1681p window dispositive, so the node would conclude the claim is time-barred (>2 years from discovery and beyond the 5-year outside limit) and that she has no viable furnisher claim. That is materially misleading: each new CRA-forwarded dispute triggers a fresh § 1681s-2(b) duty and, if the furnisher again fails to conduct a reasonable investigation of still-inaccurate information, a new violation with a new limitations period. The correct advice is 'redispute now,' not 'no claim.' The node nowhere states that the duty (and the claim) renews on each new dispute.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer co-signed her nephew's auto loan. After default, the collection agency calls the nephew (primary obligor) and also calls her, the co-signer, four times in a week, discussing the balance and demanding payment. She asks whether the calls to her were lawful.
edge_cases.gap_description: Checklist item 16 tells the analyst that any call recipient who is NOT the consumer and NOT on the 1692c(d) list (spouse, parent of a minor, guardian, executor, administrator) must be run through the 1692c(b)/1692b third-party-communication bar, which the third_party_communication_note describes as 'generally prohibitive' and 'very likely a separate, more direct FDCPA violation.' A co-signer/co-obligor is not on the 1692c(d) list and is not among the item-16 'if not' examples, so the encoding routes him there — but a co-obligor is himself a 'consumer' under 15 U.S.C. 1692a(3) ('any natural person obligated or allegedly obligated to pay any debt'), and communications with him about the debt he owes are direct consumer communications, not third-party contacts. The node's unit_of_count mentions a co-signer only for bucket-counting purposes and never corrects the third-party routing. Result: the node affirmatively tells a co-signer (or an authorized user, joint account holder, or guarantor) that she has a clean 1692c(b)/1692b claim she does not have — a wrong answer in the claim-creating direction, and a realistic one given how common co-signed auto, student and retail-card debt is.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer tells the collector by phone, 'Do not call me at work, I can get fired' and 'don't call me before 10 a.m.' The collector keeps calling her desk line four times the following week, at 8:15 a.m. Her employer has no stated policy against personal calls, and she never sent anything in writing.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats an oral 'stop calling me at work / not before 10' only as a rebuttal factor against the presumption of compliance (checklist item 9), and its cease_communication_and_representation_note frames the workplace bar exclusively as 1692c(a)(3) ('once the collector knows or has reason to know the EMPLOYER prohibits such calls') and the time bar as a fixed 8am-9pm presumption. It never encodes the consumer-specific inconvenience rule — 15 U.S.C. 1692c(a)(1) and 12 CFR 1006.6(b)(1)(i) bar communication at any time or place the collector 'knows or should know is inconvenient to the consumer,' and the consumer's own oral statement supplies that knowledge, regardless of employer policy and regardless of the 8am-9pm window. With four calls (under 7) and no employer prohibition and no written notice, this node outputs 'presumptively compliant' and its independent-bars list does not catch the violation, so a consumer with a clean, easily provable 1692c(a)(1)/1006.6(b)(1)(i) claim is told she has none. This is one of the most common fact patterns in collection-call complaints. (Adjacent to the cross-cutting 1692c screen, but the node's own text affirmatively narrows the workplace and time restrictions rather than being silent.)

edge_cases.scenario: During a Monday call the consumer says 'I can't talk now, try me later this week.' The collector treats that as prior consent and places ten more calls over the next six days, none of which she answers. She asks whether ten calls in a week is legal.
edge_cases.gap_description: exclusions_from_count states without qualification that calls placed with prior consent given directly to the collector within the following 7 days do not count, and cooldown_rule says the consent runs up to seven days and terminates only 'once the collector has the conversation' — which never happens here because she never answers. Applied as encoded, all ten calls drop out of the 7-in-7 bucket and the node outputs 'presumptively compliant.' Two things are missing: (a) the scope of the consent (a single request to be tried 'later' is not consent to ten call attempts), and (b) more importantly, the (b)(3) exclusions only remove calls from the presumption calculus — they do not immunize the calls under 12 CFR 1006.14(a)/(b)(1) or 15 U.S.C. 1692d(5), and ten unanswered calls in six days is a strong stand-alone harassment case. Nothing in presumption_type or determination tells the analyst that excluded calls still count as conduct for the underlying harassment standard; presumption_type's rebuttal discussion is framed around calls that were counted. Consumer-requested callbacks are extremely common, and collectors routinely rely on them, so the encoded rule will produce a materially wrong 'compliant' answer.

results.derivation_summary: 15 U.S.C. § 1692e broadly bars a debt collector from using any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt, and then lists sixteen non-exhaustive examples: falsely implying government affiliation or endorsement (1); misrepresenting the character, amount, or legal status of the debt, or the services/compensation of the collector (2); falsely posing as an attorney or as sending an attorney communication (3); threatening arrest, imprisonment, seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale that is unlawful or not intended (4); threatening any action that cannot legally be taken or is not intended (5); falsely implying a transfer of the debt strips the consumer of claims/defenses or subjects them to prohibited practices (6); falsely implying the consumer committed a crime or disgraceful conduct (7); communicating credit information known to be false, including failing to note a debt is disputed (8); using documents simulating court or government process or creating a false impression of source (9); using any false representation or deceptive means to collect or to obtain consumer information (10); failing to make the 'mini-Miranda' disclosures (11); falsely implying accounts went to innocent purchasers for value (12); falsely implying documents are legal process (13); using a business name other than the collector's true name (14); falsely implying documents are not legal process or require no action (15); and falsely implying the collector operates or is employed by a consumer reporting agency (16).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer receives a dunning letter on the letterhead of a real law firm, signed 'Smith & Associates, Attorneys at Law,' demanding payment and hinting at suit. The firm is genuinely a law firm, but the letter is one of 40,000 mass-generated by the collection agency's automated system; no attorney ever reviewed the consumer's file or exercised professional judgment before it went out.
edge_cases.gap_description: Catalog item (3) is encoded only as 'falsely claiming to be, or to communicate from, an attorney.' Applied literally, a letter from an actual law firm is not a match, so the node returns no violation. But the dominant line of authority (Clomon v. Jaffe, Avila v. Rubin, Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, Miller v. Wolpoff) holds that an attorney-signed collection letter sent without meaningful attorney involvement is itself a false representation under 1692e(3) and (10) — one of the highest-volume 1692e theories in practice. The node has no 'meaningful attorney involvement' gloss and the checklist never asks whether an attorney actually reviewed the account, so the consumer is told the wrong thing on a strong claim.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's letters and caller ID show 'Meridian Recovery Solutions,' but the state license and corporate registration are in the name 'ABC Financial Services, Inc.,' which has used the Meridian trade name openly and consistently for a decade and registered it as a d/b/a. The consumer asks whether the mismatched name is a violation.
edge_cases.gap_description: Catalog item (14) is encoded as a flat prohibition on 'using a business name other than the collector's true name,' which on these facts yields a false positive: a standalone 1692e(14) violation. Courts and the FTC staff commentary have long read 1692e(14) to permit a collector to use a fictitious or trade name it is commonly known by and consistently uses (the target is name-hopping and false-third-party impressions, cf. 1692j flat-rating). Trade-name/DBA use is near-universal in the industry, so the encoded item will routinely tell consumers they have a claim they do not have — the mirror-image error of the false negatives the node has already been patched for.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer phoned the collector to say 'this account isn't mine, I dispute it,' and the collector nonetheless continued furnishing the tradeline to the credit bureaus each month with no dispute flag; the consumer discovers this when a mortgage lender pulls her report. There were no threats and the letters' wording was unremarkable.
edge_cases.gap_description: Catalog item (8) (communicating known-false credit information, including failing to note a debt is disputed) is the operative theory, but the completeness checklist collects nothing about credit furnishing at all — no item asks whether the consumer disputed the debt, whether the dispute was oral or written, whether the collector furnished to a CRA after learning of it, or whether the dispute was noted. Every dispositive checklist item points at letter wording, call content, threats, and coverage, so a fact-gathering pass driven by the checklist misses this scenario entirely and returns 'no violation identified.' The oral/written distinction also matters: 1692e(8)'s dispute-notation duty is triggered by a dispute the collector knows of, unlike 1692g(b)'s writing requirement — a nuance nothing in the node captures.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's car is repossessed from her driveway at 3 a.m. by a repossession agency hired by the auto lender. The repo company does not collect payments or send dunning letters -- its only business is seizing collateral. She asks whether the FDCPA gives her a claim for the repossession, which occurred after she had already cured the default.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's debt_collector_threshold_note and the dispositive first checklist item state categorically that 'This entire node applies only if the entity is a debt collector under 1692a(6)' and that the node does not apply if that threshold fails. But 1692a(6)'s flush language provides that 'For the purpose of section 1692f(6) of this title, such term also includes any person who uses any instrumentality of interstate commerce or the mails in any business the principal purpose of which is the enforcement of security interests.' Repossession agencies and other security-interest enforcers who are NOT debt collectors for any other FDCPA purpose ARE covered for catalog item (6). The node's threshold screen would wrongly dismiss the most common item-(6) defendant out of the statute entirely; the cross-referenced coverage node is described only as covering the two principal-purpose/regular-collection tests, the (A)-(F) exclusions, and Henson -- not the 1692f(6) limited-purpose expansion.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer receives a collection letter from a third-party agency demanding the $800 principal plus a $200 'collection fee' and post-charge-off interest that her original credit-card agreement never authorized. She never paid anything -- she disputed the letter and asks whether the agency violated the FDCPA.
edge_cases.gap_description: Catalog item (1) is phrased as 'collecting any amount not expressly authorized' and the corresponding dispositive checklist item asks 'Whether any collected amount (fees, interest, charges) beyond principal was authorized.' Section 1692f in fact reaches use of unfair means 'to collect or attempt to collect any debt,' and 1692f(1) is routinely violated by a mere demand for an unauthorized amount with no payment ever made -- which is the dominant real-world 1692f(1) fact pattern. Applied literally, the encoding invites a false negative ('you never paid it, so nothing was collected') for the most common consumer presenting these facts; the node's TransUnion standing note compounds the risk by suggesting an unpaid demand is a 'bare procedural' harm.

edge_cases.scenario: An active-duty servicemember who bought his car and signed the loan before entering service falls behind; the lender's agent takes the vehicle by self-help from an open driveway with no confrontation, lock-cutting, or objection. He asks whether the repossession was lawful.
edge_cases.gap_description: Item (6) and the new repossession_breach_of_peace_note frame the 'present right to possession' analysis as (a) default under the security agreement, (b) no state-law exemption, and (c) no breach of the peace. For a servicemember whose obligation was incurred before military service, 50 U.S.C. 3952 bars ANY repossession of the vehicle during service without a court order, regardless of default and regardless of a peaceful taking -- so there is no present right to repossess nonjudicially. The encoded analysis would answer 'default plus peaceful taking equals present right, no item (6) violation,' which is affirmatively wrong for this population (the subject of repeated DOJ enforcement against major auto lenders).

results.derivation_summary: Under § 1692a(6), a person is a "debt collector" if either (a) the principal purpose of its business is collecting debts, or (b) it regularly collects, directly or indirectly, debts "owed or due another" — and a separate limited-purpose prong covers businesses whose principal purpose is enforcing security interests, but only for § 1692f(6). The Act reaches only a "debt" under § 1692a(5), i.e., a consumer's obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes; a "consumer" is the natural person obligated (expanded for § 1692c and 12 C.F.R. § 1006.6(a) to include a spouse, parent of a minor, guardian, executor/administrator, and, under Regulation F, a confirmed successor in interest). A "creditor" under § 1692a(4) is one who extends credit or is owed the debt, excluding a person taking assignment of a defaulted debt solely to collect for another; Henson holds that an entity collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not collecting debts "owed another" (leaving the principal-purpose prong unresolved), and Obduskey holds a business doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure is not a debt collector except for § 1692f(6). Section 1692a(6)(A)–(F) further excludes creditors' own employees, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons whose collection is incidental to a fiduciary/escrow role, concerns debts they originated or that were not in default when obtained, or debts obtained as a secured party in a commercial credit transaction.

results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a), a debt collector must, within five days after the initial communication (unless the information was already in that communication or the debt is paid), send a written validation notice stating: (1) the amount of the debt; (2) the name of the creditor owed; (3) that the debt will be assumed valid unless the consumer disputes it within 30 days after receipt of the notice; (4) that a written dispute within the 30-day period triggers the collector's duty to obtain and mail verification or a copy of a judgment; and (5) that a written request within that period will get the consumer the original creditor's name and address. Regulation F (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(a)(1), (c)) allows the same validation information to be given orally in the initial communication or by a written notice in or within five days of it. The dispute window is measured from receipt, not mailing: § 1006.34(b)(5) defines the 'validation period' as starting when the collector provides the validation information and ending 30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive it, and the collector may assume receipt on any date at least five days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after providing it; if an undeliverable notice is re-sent, comment 34(b)(5)-2 requires the end date to be recalculated from receipt (or assumed receipt) of the subsequent notice. During that period, a written dispute or request for the original creditor's name requires the collector to cease collection until verification/judgment or the creditor information is mailed (§ 1692g(b); § 1006.38(c)), and collection activity may otherwise continue but must not overshadow or be inconsistent with the disclosed rights (§ 1692g(b) final sentence; § 1006.38(b)(1)). Note that a formal pleading in a civil action is not an 'initial communication' triggering subsection (a) (§ 1692g(d)).

edge_cases.gap_description: The judgment_enforcement_note tells the user a California judgment is 'enforceable for 10 years from entry, renewable for additional 10-year periods without limit' and warns against telling the consumer the judgment is 'expired.' It never states that renewal must be applied for BEFORE the 10-year period runs (CCP 683.130, 683.020) and that an unrenewed judgment simply ceases to be enforceable and cannot be revived. This is a distinct problem from the sister-state dormancy issue already fixed (D-07), which concerns rendering-state law.

CCP 703.050(a) provides that whether property is exempt and the AMOUNT of the exemption are determined by the exemption statutes in effect when the judgment creditor's lien was created (or when a senior lien was created). Outside bankruptcy, a debtor whose abstract was recorded pre-2021 may be limited to the old $75k/$100k/$175k figures -- a several-hundred-thousand-dollar swing that can be the difference between 'no bid can exceed liens plus exemption' (no sale) and a forced sale. edge_cases.scenario: The debtor owns the home as a 50% tenant in common with her brother (alternatively: as community property with a non-debtor spouse), and only she is the judgment debtor. She asks whether the creditor can force a sale of the house.
edge_cases.gap_description: Nothing in the logic or checklist asks about title and co-ownership, yet it drives the answer. A creditor can reach only the debtor's fractional interest of a non-spouse co-tenant, so the 704.800 minimum-bid arithmetic must be run against the debtor's share (and the exemption is one exemption per homestead, not one per owner), whereas under Fam. Code 910 the ENTIRE community-property residence is liable for one spouse's separate debt even though the non-debtor spouse is not on the judgment. Applying the encoded rule to whole-property equity will materially overstate exposure for the unmarried co-tenant and materially understate it for the non-debtor spouse who is told 'half the house is mine and untouchable.'

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor moved to California from Nevada eight months ago, is now facing a sheriff's levy on a car with $14,000 of equity, and is considering Chapter 7. The node's bankruptcy_alternative_note tells her she may elect California's § 703.140(b) 'System 2' exemptions (~$8,625 vehicle plus wildcard/unused-homestead stacking).
edge_cases.gap_description: The bankruptcy_alternative_note affirmatively states that a Chapter 7 filer 'may instead elect' CCP § 703.140(b), with no domicile screen. Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A), a debtor who has not been domiciled in California for the 730 days before filing must use the exemptions of the state where she was domiciled for the greater part of the 180-day period preceding that 730 days (or the federal § 522(d) set if that state's exemptions are unavailable extraterritorially). For a recent transplant -- a common profile in a high-mobility state -- neither the § 704.010 $7,500 figure nor System 2 is available in her bankruptcy, so the node's own affirmative bankruptcy statement is wrong for her, not merely silent. There is no checklist item asking how long the debtor has lived in California.

edge_cases.scenario: A self-employed contractor is levied on his work truck with $5,300 of equity. Applying the node, he is told the § 704.060 tools-of-trade vehicle cap is '~$4,850' (aggregate '~$8,725'), so roughly $450 of equity is reachable; a Chapter 7 comparison is run using the note's '~$8,625 vehicle / ~$1,950 wildcard / ~$36,750 homestead' System 2 figures.
edge_cases.gap_description: All of the node's cross-referenced dollar amounts (§ 704.060 tools-of-trade, § 703.140(b) System 2 vehicle/wildcard/homestead) are hardcoded with no as-of date and no reference to CCP § 703.150, which requires the Judicial Council to adjust § 703 and § 704 exemption amounts for CPI every three years (April 1 cycle). The quoted figures track a prior adjustment cycle and understate the current caps by roughly a full adjustment. For any debtor whose equity falls between the stale and current caps, the node flips the answer from 'fully exempt' to 'partially reachable' -- an entire exemption tier, not a rounding discrepancy. The same omission means the headline $7,500 will silently go stale at the next adjustment, and there is no checklist item capturing the levy/filing date against which the correct amounts must be selected.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor's financed Honda is levied. His California Certificate of Title shows the credit union as 'legal owner' and him as 'registered owner.' Applying the checklist item 'exactly whose name(s) are on the title -- if a third party holds title (in whole or part) ... the debtor has no exemption to claim in property that is not his,' he is told the lender holds title and his exemption is limited or unavailable.
edge_cases.gap_description: The co_owner_and_third_party_title_note and its checklist item use 'title' without distinguishing California's legal-owner (lienholder) vs. registered-owner structure, which appears on essentially every financed vehicle. Read literally it points to 'no exemption / third-party claim' when the correct analysis is the FMV-minus-lien equity computation the node otherwise performs. The tension between the two paths can produce a materially wrong answer for the most common levy fact pattern (a financed car).

edge_cases.scenario: An 82-year-old whose only income is Social Security, direct-deposited to a single checking account, is levied by a debt buyer with about $6,000 in the account (several months of benefits she saved for a car repair). Using this node, she is told roughly $3,500–$5,250 of Social Security deposits are automatically exempt plus the § 704.220 minimum, so she assumes the rest is gone.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node scrupulously refuses to hardcode the § 704.220 figure but then hardcodes stale § 704.080 dollar ranges ($1,750–$2,600 / $3,500–$5,250) as 'most recently adjusted' with no look-up-current warning; the biennially adjusted amounts are now higher. More importantly, it omits 42 U.S.C. § 407(a), under which traceable Social Security funds are exempt in full without regard to the § 704.080 caps (the caps function as the automatic, no-claim floor, not the ceiling). A benefits-only debtor is told a substantial part of her account is unprotected when essentially all of it is exempt on a timely claim.

edge_cases.scenario: A father is levied by his ex-wife (or the local child support agency via a Financial Institution Data Match) on $2,400 of child-support arrears; the account holds his last paycheck and he needs it for rent. The node's carve-out tells him the automatic minimum simply 'does not apply' to support judgments.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats the wages/child-support/spousal-support carve-out as leaving the debtor with no protection at all. That is wrong: CCP § 703.070(b) provides that otherwise-exempt property is applied to a support judgment only to the extent the court determines it exceeds the amount necessary for the support of the debtor and their dependents, and § 704.070's recent-wage exemption is likewise subject to that need-based balancing rather than eliminated; a DCSS financial-institution levy also carries its own hardship/claim procedure (Fam. Code § 17453 et seq.). Support-arrears bank levies are extremely common, and telling this debtor he has zero protection and no procedure to invoke is materially misleading.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's account is frozen and she says she never knew she was sued -- the default judgment was taken by a debt buyer after service on an old address. She asks what she can protect. The node answers only with the automatic minimum plus possible exemption claims.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node presumes a valid, enforceable judgment and writ and never flags the threshold validity questions that dominate real bank-levy intakes: an unserved/defectively served default (motion to vacate under CCP §§ 473(b), 473.5, 473(d), which quashes the levy and can recover the entire seized balance), a judgment more than 10 years old never renewed (CCP §§ 683.020, 683.130), or a levy on a satisfied/vacated judgment. Steering such a consumer into an exemption claim capped at the minimum, on a 15/20-day clock, materially misdirects her away from the remedy that would return all the money -- and the checklist contains no 'is the underlying judgment valid and the writ current' item.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 412.20(a)(3), (a)(6), the summons must direct the defendant to file a written response with the court within 30 days after the summons is served, and warns the court may decide against them if they don't respond in that time. The 30 days runs from when service is deemed complete, which varies by method — e.g., substituted service and out-of-state mail service are complete on the 10th day after mailing (§§ 415.20(a), 415.40), notice-and-acknowledgment service is complete when the acknowledgment is executed and returned (§ 415.30(c)), and publication per Gov. Code § 6064 (§ 415.50(c)). If no answer, demurrer, motion to strike, or motion to quash is filed within the time specified in the summons, the clerk must enter the defendant's default on the plaintiff's application (§§ 412.20(a)(4), 585(a)). Filing a motion to quash under § 418.10 extends the time to plead until 15 days after service of written notice of the order denying it (plus up to 20 additional days for good cause), and a defendant who defaults through mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect may seek relief under § 473(b) within a reasonable time not exceeding six months.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues on a Chase credit-card account. The defendant's cardholder agreement contains an arbitration clause, and on day 20 she files a petition to compel arbitration under CCP § 1281.7 instead of an answer. She asks whether she still has to file an answer by day 30.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's universe of timely responses is answer / motion to quash / demurrer / motion to strike. It omits a petition to compel arbitration, which CCP § 1281.7 expressly permits to be filed 'in lieu of' an answer and which bars entry of default until after the petition is denied and the defendant then fails to answer within the time allowed. Arbitration clauses are near-universal in consumer credit agreements and moving to compel is a mainstream debt-defense strategy. As encoded, the rule would tell this defendant she is in default on day 31 (pushing her to file an answer, which can itself be argued to waive or complicate the arbitration right), or conversely fail to tell a defendant relying on the petition what her post-denial answer deadline is.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer files suit in Los Angeles County against a defendant who lives in Fresno County and signed the credit application there. The defendant asks what to do by day 30; she wants to fight the case but also does not want to drive 200 miles to every hearing.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node omits improper venue entirely. For consumer credit contracts, CCP § 395(b) restricts venue to the county of the defendant's residence or where the contract was signed (mirrored by 15 U.S.C. § 1692i), and CCP § 396b(a) requires the motion to transfer to be made at or before the time the defendant answers, demurs, or moves to strike -- otherwise the objection is waived. Filing wrong-county suits is a well-documented debt-buyer practice. The node's advice to 'file an answer by day 30' therefore causes the defendant to forfeit a live venue objection (and the leverage of the associated FDCPA/Rosenthal claim). This is structurally similar to, but distinct from, the pleaded-affirmative-defenses issue in D-05, since venue must be raised by noticed motion rather than in the answer's defenses.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant is personally served on a date such that day 30 falls on a Saturday (or a court holiday), and the clerk's office is closed. She asks whether she must get the answer in by that Saturday.

A default against fewer than all defendants (or not disposing of all claims) is interlocutory; the appellate/plenary clock does not start until a final judgment or severance, and the trial court may set the interlocutory default aside at any time before then on its own plenary authority. Neither the logic nor the checklist asks whether the judgment is final as to all parties and claims, so a defendant with a live, freely-revisitable interlocutory default is told her only path is closed.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is sued in Texas justice court by a collection firm on a defaulted federal Direct/FFEL student loan (or a Department of Education-assigned account) that went into default in 2016. She asks whether the four-year statute of limitations bars the suit.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node applies a flat 4-year period to any 'consumer debt' with no screen for debt types that carry no limitations period or a federal one: 20 U.S.C. § 1091a expressly abolishes all statutes of limitations for actions to collect federally guaranteed/insured student loans (and 28 U.S.C. § 2415 governs other U.S.-government contract debts, with its own carve-outs). Student-loan collection suits are a routine consumer-debt posture. As encoded, the node would report a 2016-default, 2025-filed suit as 'expired,' handing the consumer a defense that does not exist and inviting her to rely on it. Neither the logic nor the checklist asks who the original creditor was or whether the loan is federally guaranteed.

edge_cases.scenario: Consumer defaulted on a Chase card in March 2020 (charge-off November 2020). In 2023 -- inside the four years -- she signed a written hardship/payment-plan letter from the debt buyer and made three $50 payments. The debt buyer sues in 2025, more than four years after charge-off but two years after the signed plan.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node addresses only payments made AFTER the four years ran (16.065 / 392.307). It supplies no rule for a signed written acknowledgment or new promise made BEFORE expiration, which under Texas law (§ 16.065 and the new-promise/acknowledgment line of cases) starts a fresh four-year period running from the acknowledgment or the promised payment date. Structured payment plans and settlement letters inside the limitations window are standard debt-buyer practice. As encoded, accrual is fixed at default/acceleration and the 2025 suit is reported 'expired,' when the writing likely makes it timely -- the consumer is told she has a winning defense and may forgo settlement, arbitration, or merits defenses on that basis. The checklist asks only whether the payment was before or after expiration and gives no consequence for 'before.'

edge_cases.scenario: Consumer's car was repossessed after he stopped paying in January 2020; the lender accelerated in March 2020 but did not sell the vehicle at auction until October 2020. The finance company sues for the deficiency in August 2024.
edge_cases.gap_description: Auto deficiency suits are one of the most common Texas consumer-debt filings, and the node's installment note expressly invites auto loans to be run through the acceleration date. But a deficiency claim does not accrue until the collateral is disposed of and the deficiency becomes ascertainable (Bus. & Com. Code ch. 9 disposition/§ 2.725 line of cases); the gap between acceleration and the auction is routinely six months to a year. Computing from the March 2020 acceleration reports the August 2024 suit as expired when it is timely from the October 2020 sale -- the dangerous direction. Relatedly, a deficiency after a REAL-property foreclosure is governed by a two-year period (Tex. Prop. Code § 51.003), not four. Neither the checklist nor the logic asks whether collateral was repossessed/foreclosed or when it was sold.

results.derivation_summary: Under Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28, current wages for personal service can never be garnished, with the only exceptions being court-ordered child support and spousal maintenance — so garnishment for ordinary consumer debt is barred. Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004 mirrors this, directing that a garnishee be discharged as to any debt for current wages unless other state or federal law provides otherwise, and § 31.0025(a) bars courts from ordering turnover of wages before they are paid to the debtor. Related provisions confirm the narrow exceptions: an employer may withhold wages only under court order, statutory authorization, or written employee consent (Tex. Lab. Code § 61.018), and child-support withholding is capped at 50 percent of disposable earnings (Tex. Fam. Code § 158.009). Once wages are paid out, however, the constitutional protection is framed in terms of 'current wages,' and separate exemptions (e.g., Social Security under 42 U.S.C. § 407(a) and unemployment benefits under Tex. Lab. Code § 207.075) govern funds already deposited.
results.citation_used: Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28; Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 63.004, 31.0025(a)

edge_cases.scenario: A Texas debtor defaulted on federal student loans; the Department of Education's servicer issues an administrative wage garnishment order and the employer begins withholding roughly 30% of the paycheck. The debtor asks whether the garnishment is lawful.
edge_cases.gap_description: The federal_override_note states flatly that federal-law garnishments 'DO reach current Texas wages,' with no mention of the statutory caps: Dept. of Education AWG is limited to 15% of disposable pay (20 U.S.C. 1095a(a)(1)), IRS levies must leave the 26 U.S.C. 6334(a)(9)/(d) exempt amount, FDCPA garnishment on U.S. judgments is capped at 25% (28 U.S.C. 3205(a)/15 U.S.C. 1673), and the CCPA outer ceiling applies. This is exactly the defect already fixed for support withholding in D-06 (never say 'no protection'), but it remains uncorrected on the federal-override side: an over-withholding debtor would be told the garnishment is simply valid rather than that the amount above the cap is challengeable through the agency hearing process.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment creditor of one spouse serves a writ of garnishment on a bank account held jointly by the judgment debtor and his non-debtor wife (or, in another common variant, a joint account with an elderly parent), freezing funds that are the non-debtor's separate property or the non-debtor spouse's sole-management community property from her own paycheck.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node affirmatively advises that 'bank account funds CAN generally be frozen/seized' and qualifies that only for exempt-benefit deposits (D-01/D-05). It says nothing about OWNERSHIP: Tex. Fam. Code 3.202 limits which marital property is liable for which spouse's debts (a non-debtor spouse's sole-management community property is generally not liable for the other spouse's non-tortious premarital/separate debts), and a non-debtor joint account holder can assert an ownership claim in the garnishment proceeding (TRCP 664a / intervention). Applied as encoded, the rule tells a very common class of users -- households where only one spouse is sued -- that the frozen account is fair game, when a meritorious ownership defense exists and must be raised on a short deadline.

edge_cases.scenario: A collection agency repeatedly tells a Texas consumer by phone and letter that if she does not pay, it will garnish her paycheck; no suit has been filed and the debt is ordinary credit-card debt. She asks whether they can do that.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node answers only defensively ('that garnishment would be unconstitutional'), which is correct as far as it goes but leaves the user in a purely reactive posture. Threatening a Texas consumer with wage garnishment on an ordinary debt is a threat to take action that cannot legally be taken -- an affirmative claim under 15 U.S.C. 1692e(5) (and Tex. Fin. Code 392.301(a)(8)) carrying a one-year FDCPA limitations period. Because the impossibility of the threatened action is precisely what this node establishes, its silence on the resulting affirmative claim causes a common user to lose a live, time-limited remedy rather than being merely incomplete.

gaps_found_new.gap_description: The node answers only defensively ('that garnishment would be unconstitutional'), which is correct as far as it goes but leaves the user in a purely reactive posture. Threatening a Texas consumer with wage garnishment on an ordinary debt is a threat to take action that cannot legally be taken -- an affirmative claim under 15 U.S.C. 1692e(5) (and Tex. Fin. Because the impossibility of the threatened action is precisely what this node establishes, its silence on the resulting affirmative claim causes a common user to lose a live, time-limited remedy rather than being merely incomplete.

edge_cases.gap_description: The node's operative exceptions list omits refinance liens (§ 41.001(b)(5); art. XVI § 50(a)(4)). Refinanced mortgages are ubiquitous, and a refi lender's deed of trust is not literally a 'purchase-money lien.' Applied as encoded, the rule would classify a defaulted refi as an ordinary debt that cannot reach the homestead — flatly wrong and dangerous (a debtor could be told to ignore a foreclosure). The word 'refinance' appears only buried inside the hoa_lien_caveat's parenthetical recitation of § 41.001(b), not in the list the logic actually keys on, and there is no checklist item asking whether the lien is a refinance of a prior valid homestead lien.

Code § 31.002; the receiver sends the debtor a demand letter directing him to hand over his non-exempt personal property and freezes accounts through third-party demands, with receiver fees charged against the debtor. edge_cases.gap_description: The procedural note and the PROCEDURAL checklist item are framed exclusively around execution levies (TRCP 664a claim of exemption/motion to dissolve) and garnishment answers. edge_cases.scenario: A defendant finds a citation and petition taped to his front door (or receives it by certified mail) after the court authorized substituted/alternative service because the process server couldn't hand it to him personally. He counts 14 days from the day he actually found the papers and files his answer, not realizing the clock ran from the date of posting/mailing several days earlier.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node defines the trigger as 'date of service (delivery by constable or process server)' and the checklist asks only for 'the date the constable or process server delivered' the papers. It does not address substituted/alternative service (TRCP 501.2(b) in justice court; TRCP 106(b) and citation by publication in county/district court), where service is complete on the date of posting/mailing, not the date the defendant actually receives or discovers the papers. A defendant who dates the clock from discovery will be told a deadline several days too late and can default. The checklist should ask HOW service occurred and, for posted/mailed/published service, direct the user to the officer's return of service for the operative date.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues on a 'suit on sworn account' petition with an attached affidavit in a county court at law. The defendant, told his answer is due at 10:00 a.m. the Monday after 20 days, timely files a plain general-denial letter that is not sworn or verified; the plaintiff then moves for judgment on the pleadings because an unverified denial does not put a sworn account at issue.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node now expressly routes county-court defendants to the TRCP 99(b) deadline but says nothing about WHAT the answer must contain. In county/district court (unlike justice court, where TRCP 500.3(e) switches off the other rules) TRCP 185/93(10) require a sworn, verified denial to defeat a petition pleaded as a suit on sworn account -- the single most common debt-buyer pleading posture. A defendant who follows this node perfectly, files on time, and files an unverified general denial loses on the merits, which is a materially misleading outcome for a node that purports to tell a defendant how to avoid losing by default.

edge_cases.scenario: A justice-court debt-claim defendant files a timely written answer on day 12, hears nothing for two months, then receives a trial-setting notice she overlooks (or assumes the answer was the whole of her obligation) and does not appear; the court renders a post-answer judgment for the debt buyer.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats the answer as the terminal act for debt claims and, in the eviction note, expressly contrasts evictions as the case type where 'the dispositive obligation is to APPEAR at the trial setting' -- an affirmative implication that appearance is not the debt-claim defendant's obligation. Under TRCP 503.1 a debt-claim defendant who answers but fails to appear at the trial setting can have judgment rendered against her, and the 505.3 (14-day) / 506.1(a) (21-day) windows the node describes run from that judgment. Nothing in the logic or checklist flags the post-answer trial setting, so a user is left with a materially incomplete-and-misleading picture of what defeats the claim.
